To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

saving constraints interact with borrowing constraints to lower aggregate saving, reduce output, TFP and welfare, and that a mix of reforms that reduce both frictions is quantitatively more beneficial than a single strong reform.
(1) credit and saving constraints are quantitatively important, (2) the effects of these two constraints are quantitively important, (3) removing both constraints is quantitatively important.

(i) saving constraints are important in developing countries; (ii) saving constraints interact with and reinforce the effects of credit constraints; (iii) the joint presence of saving constraints and credit constraints has a negative effect on output, welfare, and the return of formal financial instruments; and (iv) a mix of moderate saving and credit constraints reforms has larger effects than a strong reform on only one of the two fronts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of saving constraints in the context of a dynamic general equilibrium model with credit constraints and heterogeneous agents.
the role of credit constraints in the transmission mechanism from monetary policy to the real economy.
the effects of credit and saving constraints on the allocation of resources and on welfare.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the model is a useful tool in understanding the role that saving and credit constraints play in a developing economy.
the model is not able to provide any conclusive statement.
saving and credit constraints have a large impact on the economy, but the impact of each constraint is difficult to isolate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the interaction between credit and saving constraints has important implications for the design of optimal financial reforms.
the combination of saving and credit constraints is a key factor in explaining the low levels of saving and output in the developing world.
saving constraints are important and that credit constraints can be important, but that the two interact in a way that makes it hard to disentangle their respective roles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
saving constraints are important in developing countries and their interaction with credit constraints can lead to large aggregate effects.
a comprehensive reform of saving and credit constraints in developing countries could have a substantial effect on the economy and welfare.
a comprehensive view of financial frictions that incorporates both saving and credit constraints is crucial to understand the impact of financial reforms on aggregate outcomes.
